title: Education: debates and issues
subtitle: selective, comprehensive, league tables, tertiary
summary: Discuss education policy in precise, formal English - equality of opportunity, selective versus comprehensive schooling, league tables, bursaries and lifelong learning.

lesson.heading: Equality of opportunity
lesson.text: Education systems are ultimately judged in terms of **equality of opportunity** - whether everyone has the same chances. The question comes up in every debate over **selective** versus **comprehensive** **schooling**: does everyone have the same chance of educational achievement, or is **elitism** of one sort or another **inherent in** the system?

examples.text: Inequality is **inherent in** the education system.
examples.note: inherent in = existing as a basic part of

examples.text: **Elitism** is bad for the country in the long term.
examples.note: elitism = favouring a small, privileged group

examples.text: **Comprehensive** education is a basic political ideal in many countries.

left.label: Selective
left.text: Pupils are chosen for entry, usually for academic reasons. In some private schools, the parents' ability to pay school fees may also be a factor.
examples: **Selective** schools choose the best students to study there.
**Selective** education means entry is decided by exam results.

right.label: Comprehensive
right.text: Everyone enters without exams and the education is free, paid for by the government.
examples: **Comprehensive** schools take all students regardless of their academic ability.
She went to the local **comprehensive** and then on to university.

lesson.heading: League tables and the two-tier system
lesson.text: **League tables** - lists of schools from the best down to the worst, based on exam results - may unintentionally help to **perpetuate** inequalities while claiming to raise standards. They divide institutions into success and failure, resulting in a **two-tier system**, or at least that is how the public **perceives** it.

examples.text: **League tables** list schools from good to bad according to their exam results.
Publishing the figures only **perpetuates** the inequalities it claims to expose.
Emphasis on the three Rs is **perceived** by parents to be the key to success.

lesson.heading: Better-off and less well-off
lesson.text: **Better-off** parents and **well-endowed** schools can push children towards the institutions at the top of the league. In the long term this may **depress** opportunity for the **less well-off** and for children from homes that do not provide the motivation to **excel**.

examples.text: A **two-tier system** of schools **depresses** the opportunities for children from **less well-off** families.
Some private schools are **well-endowed**, so they can have better resources.
examples.note: endowments = grants and gifts from rich people

examples.text: All parents want their children to **excel** at school.

lesson.note: Compound adjectives like well-off, well-endowed, high-achieving and badly-performing take comparative and superlative forms: better-off, best-endowed, higher-achieving, worst-performing.

lesson.heading: Paying for study
rows: money given to pay for studies, usually on the basis of academic merit
money given to pay for studies, usually on the basis of need
money students borrow from a bank and pay back once they are in work
education at university or college level
a student doing a first degree
a student doing a further degree

lesson.heading: Basic skills and the curriculum
lesson.text: Some people think we should return to an emphasis on the **three Rs** - reading, writing and arithmetic. **Literacy** (the ability to read) and **numeracy** (the ability to count and do basic maths) are skills no one can afford to be without. **Curriculum reform**, changes to what is covered in the national **syllabus**, is often done for political rather than educational reasons.

examples.text: Primary schools usually spend a lot of time on the **three Rs**.
Poor adult **literacy** and **numeracy** cost the economy billions.
Every government announces its own **curriculum reform** within months of taking office.

lesson.heading: Lifelong learning and special needs
lesson.text: **Lifelong** or **continuing education** - education for all ages - is a live issue, and creating opportunities for **mature students**, adult students older than the average, matters. **Special needs education** is expensive because classes must be small or **one-to-one**: one teacher and one pupil, not a group.

examples.text: There were two **mature students** in my class at university, but most of us were just 19.
At university I was lucky enough to have a lot of **one-to-one** tutorials, just me and the tutor.
**Special needs education** supports children who cannot learn in the usual way.

lesson.heading: Bullying, guidelines and distractions
lesson.text: Children are unhappy at school if there is a lot of **bullying** - threatening behaviour towards someone smaller or less powerful. Headteachers complain that **getting to grips with** constant new government **guidelines** is a **distraction** from what they ought to be focusing on.

examples.text: The report contains some interesting **guidelines** on how best to prepare for exams.
Zara's parents said a rock band would be too much of a **distraction** from her studies.
The school has a zero-tolerance policy on **bullying**.

exercises.prompt: ___ tables list schools from the best down to the worst according to their exam results.
exercises.explanation: League tables rank institutions, and critics say they create a two-tier system.

exercises.prompt: In ___ education, entry to schools is decided by exam results.
exercises.explanation: Selective schools choose their pupils; comprehensive schools take everyone.

exercises.prompt: Equality of ___ means that everyone has the same chances.
exercises.explanation: Equality of opportunity is the standard by which education systems are judged.

exercises.prompt: League tables may actually help to ___ inequalities rather than remove them.
exercises.explanation: To perpetuate something is to make it continue.

exercises.prompt: Matt won a ___ because of his excellent academic record.
exercises.explanation: A scholarship is normally awarded on merit; a bursary is awarded on need.

exercises.prompt: Katia wouldn't have gone to university if her grandparents hadn't paid her tuition ___ for her.
exercises.explanation: Tuition fees are the money paid to receive teaching.

exercises.prompt: Most undergraduates need to take out a student ___ to cover their costs while they study.
exercises.explanation: A student loan is borrowed from a bank and repaid once the student is in work.

exercises.prompt: Match each term with its definition.

pairs.right: the ability to count and do basic maths
threatening behaviour towards a weaker child
official advice on how to do something
a plan of what is to be studied

exercises.prompt: A student who is doing a doctorate is ___.
exercises.explanation: An undergraduate is doing a first degree; a postgraduate is doing a further degree.

exercises.prompt: Tertiary education is the stage that follows ___ education.
exercises.explanation: Tertiary education is study at university or college level, after secondary school.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means 'education for all ages'?
exercises.explanation: Lifelong education, also called continuing education, is education for all ages.

exercises.statement: Comprehensive schools choose the best students to study there.
exercises.explanation: Selective schools choose the best students. Comprehensive schools take all students regardless of academic ability.

exercises.statement: A well-endowed school receives a lot of money in grants and gifts.
exercises.explanation: Correct - such endowments let a school afford better resources.

Put this sentence about school policy in order.

exercises.explanation: Inherent in means existing as a basic part of something.
